plants.name: Colchicum autumnale
plants.description: Just as the garden settles into autumn, goblet-shaped blooms rise straight from bare soil. They carry no leaves, as if they had appeared by magic. Each corm sends up a cluster of delicate flowers that glow against the fallen leaves.
plants.location: Temperate Europe and gardens across the Northern Hemisphere, including North America
plants.funFact: Autumn crocus is not a true crocus. It belongs to the lily family. Its leaves appear in spring and die back long before the flowers emerge, which is why it is nicknamed 'naked ladies'.

plants.name: Symphyotrichum novae-angliae
plants.description: Tall, sturdy stems carry masses of daisy-like flowers with golden-yellow centers and rays of rich purple. In autumn meadows and along roadsides, they are a feast for late-season pollinators.
plants.location: Meadows, prairies and wet ground in eastern and central North America
plants.funFact: Migrating monarch butterflies depend on New England asters for nectar. Their fuel stops along the autumn route to Mexico often come from these flowers.

plants.name: Protea cynaroides
plants.description: Its enormous flower head looks like a crown. Layers of petal-like pink bracts surround a silky, pale center. It is South Africa's national flower and grows on the rugged slopes of the fynbos.
plants.bloomingSeason: July to October, peaking in the Southern Hemisphere's late winter and spring
plants.location: Fynbos of the southwestern and southern Cape, South Africa
plants.funFact: The king protea has a thick underground stem called a lignotuber. After wildfires, it can resprout from this stem. This helps it survive in a fire-prone landscape.
